prompt:
The numbers 1 through 9 can be arranged in the triangles labeled $a$ through $i$ illustrated in the figure so that the numbers in each of the $2 \times 2$ triangles sum to the same value $n$; that is
$$a + b + c + d = b + e + f + g = d + g + h + i = n.$$
For each possible sum $n$, show such an arrangement, labeled with the sum as shown in the figure. Prove that there are no possible arrangements for any other values of $n$.

solutions.title: Bound $n$, then rule out 18 and 22
solutions.body:
**Bounds.** Adding the three equations, every cell is counted once except $b$, $d$, $g$, which lie in two of the $2\times 2$ triangles and are counted twice:
$$3n = (a + b + \dots + i) + (b + d + g) = 45 + (b + d + g).$$
Since $b, d, g$ are three distinct numbers from 1 to 9, $6 \le b + d + g \le 24$, so $51 \le 3n \le 69$ and $17 \le n \le 23$.

**Examples.** Writing an arrangement as $(a;\ b, c, d;\ e, f, g, h, i)$ (top row; middle row; bottom row, left to right):

| $n$ | arrangement | checks |
|---|---|---|
| 17 | $(9;\ 3, 4, 1;\ 5, 7, 2, 6, 8)$ | $9+3+4+1 = 3+5+7+2 = 1+2+6+8 = 17$ |
| 19 | $(6;\ 1, 8, 4;\ 9, 2, 7, 3, 5)$ | $6+1+8+4 = 1+9+2+7 = 4+7+3+5 = 19$ |
| 20 | $(1;\ 7, 9, 3;\ 6, 2, 5, 4, 8)$ | $1+7+9+3 = 7+6+2+5 = 3+5+4+8 = 20$ |
| 21 | $(2;\ 3, 7, 9;\ 8, 4, 6, 5, 1)$ | $2+3+7+9 = 3+8+4+6 = 9+6+5+1 = 21$ |
| 23 | $(4;\ 9, 3, 7;\ 1, 5, 8, 6, 2)$ | $4+9+3+7 = 9+1+5+8 = 7+8+6+2 = 23$ |

**$n = 18$ is impossible.** Then $b + d + g = 3\cdot 18 - 45 = 9$. The number 9 cannot be one of $b, d, g$ (the other two would sum to 0). So 9 is one of the six cells $a, c, e, f, h, i$, and each of these lies in exactly one $2\times2$ triangle. That small triangle consists of the cell with 9, one more unshared cell $x$, and two of $b, d, g$; call the third of $b, d, g$ (the one not in this triangle) $z$. Its sum is
$$18 = 9 + x + (9 - z),$$
so $x = z$ — two different cells with the same number, a contradiction. (For instance, if 9 is in $a$ or $c$, the triangle is $\{a, b, c, d\}$ and $z = g$.)

**$n = 22$ is impossible.** Replacing every entry $x$ by $10 - x$ turns an arrangement with sum $n$ into one with sum $40 - n$ (each small triangle has 4 cells). A sum-22 arrangement would give a sum-18 arrangement, which does not exist.

Hence the possible sums are exactly $17, 19, 20, 21, 23$. ∎

solutions.title: Case check for $n = 18$
solutions.body:
As a check of the key step, list the possibilities directly. For $n = 18$, $\{b, d, g\}$ is a 3-element set with sum 9: $\{1,2,6\}$, $\{1,3,5\}$ or $\{2,3,4\}$, and by the 3-fold rotational symmetry of the figure (which permutes $b, d, g$ and the three small triangles) we may fix the order.

* $b = 4, d = 2, g = 3$: $a + c = 18 - 6 = 12$ with numbers other than $2, 3, 4$ forces $\{a, c\} = \{5, 7\}$ (as $3 + 9$ and $4 + 8$ are excluded); and $e + f = 18 - 7 = 11$ forces $\{e, f\} = \{5, 6\}$ (as $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ are excluded) — 5 is used twice.
* $b = 1, d = 5, g = 3$: $\{a, c\}$ sums to 12 avoiding $1,3,5$: $\{4, 8\}$. Then $h + i = 10$ avoiding $1,3,5,4,8$: needs $\{2, 8\}$ or $\{4,6\}$ — both reuse a number.
* $b = 1, d = 2, g = 6$: $a + c = 15$ gives $\{7, 8\}$; $e + f = 11$ gives $\{3, 8\}$ or $\{4, 7\}$ — conflict.

Every case fails, confirming $n \ne 18$; by the $x \mapsto 10 - x$ symmetry $n \ne 22$. A computer search over all $9!$ arrangements also finds exactly the sums $17, 19, 20, 21, 23$. ∎

prompt:
Call a number $a - b\sqrt2$ with $a$ and $b$ both positive integers *tiny* if it is closer to zero than any number $c - d\sqrt2$ such that $c$ and $d$ are positive integers with $c < a$ and $d < b$. Three numbers which are tiny are $1 - \sqrt2$, $3 - 2\sqrt2$, and $7 - 5\sqrt2$. Without using a calculator or computer, prove whether or not each of the following is tiny:

(a) $58 - 41\sqrt2$, (b) $99 - 70\sqrt2$.
answer: (a) **Not tiny**: $|58 - 41\sqrt2| = \sqrt2\,|41 - 29\sqrt2| > |41 - 29\sqrt2|$. (b) **Tiny**: $99^2 - 2\cdot70^2 = 1$, so a closer $c - d\sqrt2$ with $c < 99$, $d < 70$ would give $0 < |c^2 - 2d^2| < 1$.

solutions.title: Multiply by $\sqrt2$ and by conjugates
solutions.body:
**(a)** Multiply $41 - 29\sqrt2$ by $\sqrt2$:
$$\sqrt2\,(41 - 29\sqrt2) = 41\sqrt2 - 58 = -(58 - 41\sqrt2).$$
So $|58 - 41\sqrt2| = \sqrt2\,|41 - 29\sqrt2| > |41 - 29\sqrt2|$ (the number $41 - 29\sqrt2$ is not zero since $\sqrt2$ is irrational). As $41 < 58$ and $29 < 41$, the number $41 - 29\sqrt2$ is a closer competitor, so $58 - 41\sqrt2$ is **not tiny**.

**(b)** Note $99^2 - 2\cdot 70^2 = 9801 - 9800 = 1$, i.e. $(99 - 70\sqrt2)(99 + 70\sqrt2) = 1$. Suppose $c, d$ are positive integers with $c < 99$, $d < 70$ and $|c - d\sqrt2| < |99 - 70\sqrt2|$. Then, since $0 < c + d\sqrt2 < 99 + 70\sqrt2$,
$$|c^2 - 2d^2| = |c - d\sqrt2|\,(c + d\sqrt2) < |99 - 70\sqrt2|\,(99 + 70\sqrt2) = 1.$$
But $c^2 - 2d^2$ is an integer, so it is $0$, i.e. $\sqrt2 = c/d$ would be rational — impossible. Hence no such $c, d$ exist, and $99 - 70\sqrt2$ is **tiny**. ∎

solutions.title: Powers of $1 - \sqrt2$
solutions.body:
The given tiny numbers are powers of $1 - \sqrt2$:
$$(1-\sqrt2)^2 = 3 - 2\sqrt2,\quad (1-\sqrt2)^3 = 7 - 5\sqrt2,\quad (1 - \sqrt2)^4 = 17 - 12\sqrt2,$$
$$(1-\sqrt2)^5 = 41 - 29\sqrt2,\quad (1-\sqrt2)^6 = 99 - 70\sqrt2.$$
(Multiply by $1 - \sqrt2$ each time: $(p - q\sqrt2)(1 - \sqrt2) = (p + 2q) - (p + q)\sqrt2$.)

For any $a - b\sqrt2$ with $a^2 - 2b^2 = \pm1$, the argument of part (b) above works verbatim: a closer number $c - d\sqrt2$ with smaller $c, d$ would make $|c^2 - 2d^2| < 1$. So all of these are tiny, in particular $99 - 70\sqrt2$.

On the other hand $58^2 - 2\cdot 41^2 = 3364 - 3362 = 2$, and $58 - 41\sqrt2 = \sqrt2\,(29\sqrt2 - 41)$, which is $\sqrt2$ times (in absolute value) the earlier number $41 - 29\sqrt2 = (1-\sqrt2)^5$. So it is beaten by $41 - 29\sqrt2$ and is **not tiny**. (In the language of continued fractions, the tiny numbers come exactly from the convergents $\frac11, \frac32, \frac75, \frac{17}{12}, \frac{41}{29}, \frac{99}{70}, \dots$ of $\sqrt2$, and $\frac{58}{41}$ is not one of them.) ∎

prompt: A set is *reciprocally whole* if its elements are distinct integers greater than 1 and the sum of the reciprocals of all those elements is exactly 1. Find a set $S$, as small as possible, that contains two reciprocally whole subsets, $I$ and $J$, which are distinct but not necessarily disjoint (meaning they may share elements, but they may not be the same subset). Prove that no set with fewer elements than $S$ can contain two reciprocally whole subsets.
answer: The minimum size is 5, e.g. $S = \{2, 3, 6, 7, 42\}$ with $I = \{2, 3, 6\}$, $J = \{2, 3, 7, 42\}$ (or $S = \{2,3,4,6,12\}$ with $\{2,3,6\}$, $\{2,4,6,12\}$). With 4 elements the two subsets would both have 3 elements, sharing two, which forces the third elements to be equal.

solutions.title: Size argument
solutions.body:
**A 5-element example.** $S = \{2, 3, 6, 7, 42\}$ contains
$$I = \{2, 3, 6\}:\ \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac16 = 1,\qquad J = \{2, 3, 7, 42\}:\ \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac17 + \tfrac1{42} = \tfrac{21 + 14 + 6 + 1}{42} = 1.$$

**No smaller set works.**

1. A reciprocally whole set has at least 3 elements: one element $x > 1$ gives $\frac1x < 1$, and two distinct elements give at most $\frac12 + \frac13 = \frac56 < 1$.
2. If $I \subsetneq J$ were both reciprocally whole, the reciprocal sum of $J$ would exceed that of $I$, which is 1. So neither of $I, J$ contains the other. In particular, neither can be all of $S$.
3. Hence $I$ and $J$ are proper subsets of $S$ with at least 3 elements each, so $|S| \ge 4$. Suppose $|S| = 4$. Then $I$ and $J$ are two different 3-element subsets of $S$, so they share exactly two elements: $I = \{a, b, c\}$, $J = \{a, b, d\}$ with $c \ne d$. Then
$$\tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1c = 1 = \tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1d \implies c = d,$$
a contradiction.

So the smallest possible $S$ has 5 elements, e.g. $\{2, 3, 6, 7, 42\}$. ∎

solutions.title: Classify small reciprocally whole sets
solutions.body:
Another route is to find all reciprocally whole sets with at most 3 elements. With elements $a < b < c$ and $\frac1a + \frac1b + \frac1c = 1$: since $\frac1a$ is the largest term, $\frac1a > \frac13$, so $a = 2$; then $\frac1b + \frac1c = \frac12$ with $\frac1b > \frac14$ gives $b = 3$ and $c = 6$. So $\{2, 3, 6\}$ is the **only** reciprocally whole set with at most 3 elements (none have 1 or 2 elements, as shown above).

In a set $S$ with $|S| \le 4$, the two reciprocally whole subsets cannot be $S$ itself (a proper reciprocally whole subset of a reciprocally whole set is impossible), so both have at most 3 elements — both would have to be $\{2, 3, 6\}$, contradicting $I \ne J$. Hence $|S| \ge 5$, and $S = \{2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}$ works: $\{2, 3, 6\}$ and $\{2, 4, 6, 12\}$ ($\frac{6 + 3 + 2 + 1}{12} = 1$). ∎

prompt: How many quadrilaterals in the plane have four of the nine points $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(0, 2)$, $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(1, 2)$, $(2, 0)$, $(2, 1)$, $(2, 2)$ as vertices? Do count both concave and convex quadrilaterals, but do not count figures where two sides cross each other or where a vertex angle is $180^\circ$. Rigorously verify that no quadrilateral was skipped or counted more than once.

solutions.title: Count point sets, then quadrilaterals per set
solutions.body:
**Usable 4-point sets.** There are $\binom94 = 126$ ways to choose 4 of the points. A choice containing three collinear points $P, Q, R$ (with $Q$ between $P$ and $R$) gives no valid quadrilateral: if $Q$ is joined to both $P$ and $R$, the angle at $Q$ is $180^\circ$; otherwise $P$ and $R$ are adjacent, so the side $PR$ passes through the vertex $Q$ and two sides overlap. The 3×3 grid has exactly 8 lines through three of the points (3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals), no line contains 4, and two different such lines share at most one point, so a 4-set contains at most one collinear triple. Hence the bad 4-sets number $8 \cdot 6 = 48$ (a line, plus one of the 6 other points), leaving $126 - 48 = 78$ sets with no three collinear.

**Quadrilaterals per set.** Four points, no three collinear, can be joined into a closed path in 3 ways (the 3 ways to split them into two "diagonal" pairs).
* If the four points are in convex position, exactly one of the 3 paths is non-self-intersecting (the convex quadrilateral); the other two cross.
* If one point lies inside the triangle of the other three, all 3 paths are simple (concave) quadrilaterals.

**Sets with a point inside the triangle of the others.** In the 3×3 grid the only point that can lie strictly inside a triangle of grid points is the centre $(1,1)$ (any other point lies on the boundary of the square, so it cannot be interior to a triangle contained in the square). The triangles of grid points containing $(1,1)$ in their interior, with no three of the four points collinear, are:
* one side of the square plus the midpoint of the opposite side, e.g. $(0,0), (2,0), (1,2)$: 4 triangles;
* a corner plus the midpoints of the two far sides, e.g. $(0,0), (2,1), (1,2)$: 4 triangles.

(A triangle using two opposite corners or two opposite midpoints has $(1,1)$ on a side, which is excluded; checking the remaining triangles of grid points leaves just these two families.) That makes 8 such sets.

**Total.** $70$ sets give one quadrilateral each and $8$ sets give three each:
$$70 \cdot 1 + 8 \cdot 3 = 94.$$
Each quadrilateral is counted once, since it is determined by its vertex set together with its cyclic order.

**Answer: 94**

prompt: Two circles of equal radius can tightly fit inside right triangle $ABC$, which has $AB = 13$, $BC = 12$, and $CA = 5$, in the three positions illustrated below. Determine the radii of the circles in each case.

solutions.title: Similar triangles and incircles
solutions.body:
Let $r$ be the common radius. The right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $C$) has inradius $\frac{5 + 12 - 13}{2} = 2$; any triangle similar to it with ratio $k$ has inradius $2k$.

In each case draw the common internal tangent line of the two circles (through their touching point, perpendicular to the line of centres).

**Case (i)** (both circles on $BC$). The two centres are at height $r$ above $BC$, so the common tangent is perpendicular to $BC$; it meets $BC$ at $D$ and $AB$ at $E$, with $DC = 2r$ (it is at distance $r$ from the circle next to $C$, which touches $AC$). The left circle is the incircle of $\triangle EBD \sim \triangle ABC$ with ratio $\frac{BD}{BC} = \frac{12 - 2r}{12}$. So
$$r = 2\cdot\frac{12 - 2r}{12} \implies 6r = 12 - 2r \implies r = \tfrac32.$$

**Case (ii)** (both circles on $CA$). Now the tangent is parallel to $BC$, meets $CA$ at $D$ with $CD = 2r$, and the upper circle is the incircle of $\triangle AED \sim \triangle ABC$ with ratio $\frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{5 - 2r}{5}$:
$$r = 2\cdot\frac{5 - 2r}{5} \implies 5r = 10 - 4r \implies r = \tfrac{10}{9}.$$

**Case (iii)** (one circle touches $BC$, the other $CA$, both touch $AB$). The common tangent is perpendicular to $AB$, hitting $AB$ at $D$, $BC$ at $E$ and line $AC$ at $F$. The two circles are the incircles of right triangles $EBD$ and $FAD$, both similar to $ABC$. Equal incircles mean $\triangle EBD \cong \triangle FAD$; matching the angle at $B$ in $EBD$ with the angle $\angle AFD = \angle B$ in $FAD$, the leg $DE$ (opposite $\angle B$) corresponds to the leg $AD$ (opposite $\angle F$), so $AD = DE = x$. In $\triangle EBD$: $\frac{DE}{BD} = \tan B = \frac{5}{12}$, so
$$\frac{x}{13 - x} = \frac{5}{12} \implies 17x = 65 \implies x = \tfrac{65}{17}.$$
The ratio of $\triangle EBD$ to $\triangle ABC$ is $\frac{DE}{CA} = \frac{x}{5} = \frac{13}{17}$, so $r = 2\cdot\frac{13}{17} = \frac{26}{17}$.

**Answer: (i) $\frac32$, (ii) $\frac{10}{9}$, (iii) $\frac{26}{17}$**

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $C = (0, 0)$, $B = (-12, 0)$, $A = (0, 5)$. The hypotenuse is $5x - 12y + 60 = 0$, and a point inside the triangle at distance $r$ from it satisfies $5x - 12y + 60 = 13r$.

* **(i)** Centres $(-r, r)$ (touching both legs) and $(-3r, r)$ (touching $BC$ and $AB$): $-15r - 12r + 60 = 13r$, so $r = \frac{60}{40} = \frac32$.
* **(ii)** Centres $(-r, r)$ and $(-r, 3r)$, the upper one touching $AB$: $-5r - 36r + 60 = 13r$, so $r = \frac{60}{54} = \frac{10}{9}$.
* **(iii)** Centre $P = (x_1, r)$ touches $BC$ and $AB$: $5x_1 - 12r + 60 = 13r$, so $x_1 = 5r - 12$. Centre $Q = (-r, y_2)$ touches $CA$ and $AB$: $-5r - 12y_2 + 60 = 13r$, so $y_2 = 5 - \frac32 r$. Tangency $PQ = 2r$:
$$(6r - 12)^2 + \left(\tfrac52 r - 5\right)^2 = 4r^2 \iff (2 - r)^2\left(36 + \tfrac{25}{4}\right) = 4r^2 \iff \tfrac{13}{2}(2 - r) = 2r,$$
so $r = \frac{26}{17}$.

**Answer: (i) $\frac32$, (ii) $\frac{10}{9}$, (iii) $\frac{26}{17}$**
